mainEntity.name: What is exception handling in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Exception handling in Java is the mechanism that allows a program to detect, respond to, and recover from runtime errors — called exceptions — without crashing. Java uses a structured try-catch-finally model: code that might throw is placed in the try block, catch blocks handle specific exception types, and the finally block executes regardless of whether an exception occurred (used for cleanup). This separates error-handling code from normal business logic, making programs more readable, robust, and maintainable.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Checked exceptions (subclasses of Exception but NOT RuntimeException) must be either caught or declared in the method signature with throws. The compiler enforces this — code won't compile otherwise. Examples: IOException, SQLException, ParseException. They represent recoverable conditions — things the caller can reasonably handle. Unchecked exceptions (subclasses of RuntimeException or Error) do not require catching or declaring. The compiler doesn't check them. Examples: NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, IllegalArgumentException. They typically represent programming errors or unrecoverable JVM conditions.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between throw and throws in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: throw is a statement that actually THROWS an exception at runtime — it interrupts normal flow and passes the exception to the nearest matching catch: throw new IllegalArgumentException('Invalid input'). throws is a keyword in a method signature that DECLARES which checked exceptions the method might propagate to its caller: public void readFile(String path) throws IOException. throw is used once (single exception); throws can list multiple: throws IOException, SQLException. throw creates and fires the exception; throws warns the caller to handle it.

Try-with-resources (Java 7+) is a try statement that declares one or more resources in its header. Resources are objects that implement AutoCloseable or Closeable. Java automatically calls close() on each resource when the try block exits — whether normally or via exception — in REVERSE order of declaration. This eliminates the verbose and error-prone try-catch-finally pattern previously needed to close streams, connections, and files. Example: try (FileInputStream fis = new FileInputStream(path); BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(fis))) { ... } — both are closed automatically.

mainEntity.name: Does finally always execute in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Almost always. The finally block executes after try (and catch if applicable) completes — whether normally, via exception, via return, break, or continue. The three rare exceptions where finally does NOT execute: (1) System.exit() is called inside try or catch — it terminates the JVM immediately. (2) The JVM crashes (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError at JVM level). (3) The thread executing the try block is killed forcibly. In normal application code, finally always runs. This is why it's used for resource cleanup — connection.close(), lock.unlock(), etc.

sections.title: What is an Exception in Java?

blocks.text: An exception in Java is an event that disrupts the normal flow of program execution at runtime. It is not a compile-time problem — the code compiles perfectly — but when the program runs, an unexpected condition arises: a file is missing, a network times out, a user passes a null where an object was expected, or the program attempts to divide by zero. Without a mechanism to handle these, the program simply crashes with a stack trace.

Java models exceptions as objects. When an exception occurs, the JVM creates an instance of the appropriate exception class, populates it with a message, the current stack trace, and optionally a cause — and then throws it. The runtime searches the call stack for a matching catch block. If one is found, execution jumps to that handler. If none is found anywhere in the call stack, the default exception handler terminates the thread and prints the stack trace.

Java's exception handling has two core goals: separation of concerns (keep error-handling code away from business logic) and structured recovery (give the program a chance to clean up resources and communicate failure meaningfully, rather than simply crashing). Done well, exception handling makes code significantly more readable, maintainable, and resilient.

blocks.title: 🔑 Java Exception Handling at a Glance
blocks.text: Five keywords govern Java exception handling: try (marks code that might throw), catch (handles a specific exception type), finally (always-runs cleanup block), throw (manually fires an exception), throws (method signature declaration for checked exceptions). Four constructs: try-catch, try-catch-finally, try-finally, try-with-resources (Java 7+). Two categories: checked (compiler-enforced) and unchecked (runtime, not enforced).

sections.title: Exception Hierarchy — The Throwable Family Tree

blocks.text: Every throwable object in Java descends from java.lang.Throwable. Understanding the hierarchy is essential — it explains why some exceptions must be caught, why others cannot be caught (or shouldn't be), and how a catch(Exception e) block differs from catch(Throwable t).

blocks.label: ExceptionHierarchy — The Complete Tree
lines: ├── java.lang.Error                    ← JVM-level problems — do NOT catch
│   ├── OutOfMemoryError               ← JVM ran out of heap memory
│   ├── StackOverflowError             ← Infinite recursion consumed call stack
│       └── NoClassDefFoundError       ← Class found at compile time but not runtime
├── java.lang.RuntimeException    ← UNCHECKED — compiler does not enforce
│   ├── ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException ← Array index out of range
│   ├── IllegalStateException     ← Method called at wrong time
│   ├── IndexOutOfBoundsException ← General index out of range
│   └── NoSuchElementException    ← Iterator has no more elements

blocks.title: ⚠️ Error vs Exception — A Critical Distinction
blocks.text: Error represents serious JVM-level problems that applications generally cannot and should not try to recover from: OutOfMemoryError (heap full), StackOverflowError (infinite recursion), VirtualMachineError (JVM itself is broken). Never catch Error in normal application code — catching OutOfMemoryError and continuing almost never works because the JVM is in an undefined state. Exception, by contrast, represents conditions that a well-written application can reasonably handle or at least report meaningfully.

sections.title: Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions — The Compiler's Contract

blocks.text: Java's most debated design decision is the checked exception system. Checked exceptions force the compiler to ensure every caller either handles or explicitly propagates certain exceptions. The philosophy: some failures (missing file, network unavailable, DB connection failed) are foreseeable — the API designer says 'caller: you MUST think about this failure path.' Unchecked exceptions represent programming errors or unrecoverable states that callers typically cannot fix.

sections.title: try-catch Block — Basic Syntax & Execution Flow

blocks.text: The try-catch block is the foundation of Java exception handling. Code that might throw an exception goes inside the try block. If an exception is thrown, the JVM immediately stops executing the try block at the point of the exception (remaining statements in the try block are skipped) and searches for a matching catch block. If a match is found, that handler executes and then program execution continues normally after the entire try-catch construct.

blocks.title: 💡 Execution Flow — What Gets Skipped
blocks.text: When an exception is thrown inside a try block, all remaining statements in that try block are IMMEDIATELY skipped — they never execute. Only the matching catch block runs, and then execution resumes after the entire try-catch (or try-catch-finally). This means: if your try block has 10 lines and line 3 throws, lines 4-10 are skipped. Design your code so that partially-executed operations don't leave the system in an inconsistent state — or use finally/try-with-resources for cleanup.

sections.title: Multiple catch Blocks — The Specificity Ladder

blocks.text: A single try block can have multiple catch blocks, each handling a different exception type. Java evaluates them top-to-bottom and executes the first matching catch block — all subsequent catch blocks are skipped. This creates a critical ordering rule: more specific exceptions must come before less specific ones. Placing a superclass catch block before a subclass causes a compile error.

// Most specific IOException subclass — must come BEFORE IOException
System.err.println("Please check the file path and try again.");
// General I/O failure — comes AFTER FileNotFoundException
System.err.println("'" + numberStr + "' is not a valid integer.");
System.err.println("Cannot divide by zero. Provide a non-zero number.");
// Catch-all — most general, MUST come last
} catch (IOException e) {          // IOException is superclass of
} catch (FileNotFoundException e) { // ❌ COMPILE ERROR — already caught above!

blocks.title: ⚠️ The Unreachable Catch Block — Compile Error
blocks.text: If you place catch(IOException e) before catch(FileNotFoundException e), the compiler throws an error: 'exception FileNotFoundException has already been caught'. This is Java's compile-time enforcement of the specificity rule. Always order catch blocks from MOST SPECIFIC (deepest subclass) to LEAST SPECIFIC (shallowest superclass). The golden rule: if ExceptionA is a subclass of ExceptionB, ExceptionA's catch block must appear BEFORE ExceptionB's.

sections.title: Multi-catch (Java 7+) — One Block, Many Exception Types

blocks.text: Java 7 introduced multi-catch — a single catch block that handles multiple unrelated exception types using the pipe (|) operator. This is ideal when different exception types require the same handling logic — eliminating code duplication without compromising specificity. Multi-catch is a pure syntax improvement: at bytecode level it generates the same structure as separate catch blocks.

blocks.label: MultiCatch.java
lines: // ❌ BEFORE Java 7 — repetitive catch blocks with identical handling

blocks.title: 📌 Multi-catch: 'e' is Effectively Final
blocks.text: In a multi-catch block, the exception variable (e) is implicitly final — you cannot reassign it inside the block. This is a deliberate compiler constraint: because 'e' could represent different types at runtime, reassigning it to a different exception type would be type-unsafe. The compiler enforces this: catch (IOException | SQLException e) { e = new RuntimeException(); } causes a compile error. This is different from a regular single-type catch block where reassignment is technically allowed (though bad practice).

The finally block is a block of code that always executes after the try block completes — whether it completed normally, threw an exception that was caught, threw an exception that was not caught, or exited via return, break, or continue. It is Java's mechanism for guaranteed cleanup: releasing resources, closing connections, releasing locks, or resetting state — regardless of what happened in the try block.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Never return or throw from a finally Block
blocks.text: Two dangerous finally patterns: (1) return inside finally overrides any return in try or catch — the try/catch return value is silently discarded. This masks exceptions and produces confusing behaviour. (2) throw inside finally suppresses any exception thrown in the try block — the original exception is silently lost. Both patterns hide the real cause of failures and make debugging nearly impossible. Only use finally for resource release — no return, no throw, no business logic.

Introduced in Java 7, try-with-resources is the modern, correct way to manage resources that must be closed after use. Any object implementing java.lang.AutoCloseable (or its subinterface java.io.Closeable) can be declared in the try header — Java guarantees that close() is called on each resource when the block exits, in reverse order of declaration, whether the block completes normally or via exception. This is strictly superior to manually-coded try-finally for resource management.

blocks.title: 📌 Suppressed Exceptions — What try-with-resources Does Differently
blocks.text: If both the try body AND the close() method throw exceptions, try-with-resources keeps the PRIMARY exception (from the try body) and SUPPRESSES the secondary exception (from close()). The suppressed exception is attached to the primary and accessible via e.getSuppressed(). This is better than a plain finally block where a throw in finally silently LOSES the original exception. You can inspect suppressed exceptions: for (Throwable suppressed : e.getSuppressed()) { log(suppressed); }.

The throw keyword explicitly throws an exception from your code — interrupting the current execution flow at that point. It is used to signal that a method's precondition has been violated, a business rule has been broken, or an operation cannot proceed due to an invalid state. You can throw any instance of Throwable, but in practice you always throw Exception subclasses — never Error subclasses.

It is a contract: 'I, this method, might produce these exception types — caller, you must deal with them.' It does NOT handle the exception — it propagates it up the call stack. The compiler requires this declaration for checked exceptions; it is optional but recommended for unchecked exceptions when they are part of the documented API contract.

blocks.text: Standard Java exceptions are general-purpose — IOException tells you something went wrong with I/O but not what or why in your domain. Custom exceptions give your application its own error vocabulary: InsufficientFundsException, UserNotFoundException, PaymentGatewayException. They carry domain-specific data, produce meaningful log messages, and allow callers to handle specific failure types precisely.

items.title: Rule 1 — Extend the Right Base
items.text: For checked exceptions (callers must handle): extend Exception. For unchecked (programming errors / domain invariants): extend RuntimeException. For errors the JVM should never recover from: extend Error (almost never done in application code). Modern preference: lean towards RuntimeException subclasses — most frameworks (Spring, Hibernate) use unchecked exceptions to avoid cluttering service interfaces with checked exception declarations.

items.title: Rule 2 — Provide All Four Constructors
items.text: Always provide: (1) Exception(String message), (2) Exception(String message, Throwable cause), (3) Exception(Throwable cause), (4) Exception() — the no-arg. These mirror the standard Java exception pattern. The cause constructors are critical for exception chaining — wrapping a lower-level exception in a domain exception without losing the original stack trace.

items.title: Rule 3 — Carry Domain-Specific Context
items.text: The best custom exceptions carry more than just a string message — they carry the DOMAIN DATA that caused the failure. InsufficientFundsException should carry the available balance and requested amount. UserNotFoundException should carry the userId that wasn't found. This data enables logging systems, monitoring tools, and error handlers to produce actionable alerts without parsing string messages.

items.title: Rule 4 — Make Fields Final and Immutable
items.text: Exception fields should be final — exceptions are value objects representing a single failure event. Making fields mutable allows them to be modified after creation, which destroys the immutability invariant and creates debugging nightmares. Always set all custom fields in the constructor and provide only getters.

sections.title: Exception Chaining — Preserving the Root Cause

blocks.text: Exception chaining (also called exception wrapping) is the practice of catching a lower-level exception and rethrowing a higher-level exception that wraps the original as its cause. This is critical for production debugging: the high-level exception tells you what failed at the domain level; the chained cause tells you why at the infrastructure level — without exposing implementation details to the caller.

throw new RuntimeException(e);  // AND rethrown — logged again by caller
// ✅ GOOD: Wrap with cause — original stack trace fully preserved
// 'e' becomes the cause — full chain preserved in stack trace

blocks.title: 💡 The Log-Once Rule for Exception Chaining
blocks.text: A common anti-pattern: log the exception at every level where it is caught and rethrown — leading to 3-4 identical stack traces in your logs for one failure event. The rule: log the exception ONCE, at the highest level where you can handle it (typically the service boundary, REST controller, or message consumer). At every intermediate layer: wrap with cause and rethrow, but do NOT log. The top-level handler logs once with the full chain. This keeps logs clean and searchable.

sections.title: Exception vs Error — Know the Boundary

blocks.text: Both Exception and Error extend Throwable, but they represent fundamentally different situations with different handling strategies. Understanding this boundary prevents a class of serious bugs: catching Error (or Throwable) and attempting to continue when the JVM is in an inconsistent state.

sections.title: Bad Practices & Anti-Patterns — What Causes Silent Failures

blocks.text: Exception-handling anti-patterns are uniquely dangerous because they convert loud, visible failures into silent, invisible ones. A program that crashes with a stack trace is bad. A program that swallows exceptions and silently continues with incorrect data is far worse — it corrupts business-critical information while reporting success. These are the most common exception handling failures in production Java code.

items.title: Swallowing Exceptions (Empty catch Block)
items.text: catch (Exception e) { } is the single most dangerous pattern in Java. The exception is caught, completely ignored, and execution continues as if nothing happened. The program may produce incorrect results for hours or days before anyone notices. Minimum: always log. Better: log + rethrow, or log + return a safe default that signals failure to the caller.

items.title: Catching Exception or Throwable Too Broadly
items.text: catch (Exception e) in a business method catches NullPointerException, ClassCastException, and IndexOutOfBoundsException — programming bugs that should be fixed, not silently handled. Broad catches hide real bugs. Rule: catch only the specific exception types you know how to handle. If you need a safety net, catch Exception at the outermost boundary only — never deep inside business logic.

items.title: Using Exceptions for Flow Control
items.text: try { return map.get(key); } catch (NullPointerException e) { return default; } is an abuse of exceptions. Exceptions are for EXCEPTIONAL conditions — rare, unexpected failures. Checking whether a key exists (map.containsKey(key)) is normal flow, not exceptional. Using exceptions for expected conditions is slow (exception creation builds a stack trace — expensive), unreadable, and misleading.

items.title: Logging AND Rethrowing (Double Logging)
items.text: catch (Exception e) { log.error('Failed', e); throw e; } causes the same exception to be logged 2-3 times in a layered application. Log files become unreadable — the same error appears in service layer, repository layer, and controller layer logs. Rule: log ONCE at the boundary where you actually HANDLE the exception (not just rethrow). Every other layer just wraps and rethrows.

items.title: Returning null from a catch Block
items.text: catch (Exception e) { return null; } shifts the error handling problem to the caller — but without the exception context. The caller gets null back with no indication of why, leading to a NullPointerException far from the original failure. If you must return a value from a catch block, use Optional.empty() or a Result/Either type to communicate failure explicitly.

items.title: Using Exception Message Parsing for Logic
items.text: catch (Exception e) { if (e.getMessage().contains('duplicate key')) { ... } } is fragile and wrong. Exception messages are human-readable strings — they change between DB drivers, JVM versions, and locale settings. Instead: catch the specific exception type (SQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException), check the SQL error code (e.getErrorCode()), or better yet, check the constraint BEFORE attempting the operation.

sections.title: Java Try-Catch Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions appear in Java developer interviews from fresher to senior level, in OCPJP certification exams, and in technical design discussions about error handling strategy.

items.q: Q1. What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions in Java?
items.a: Checked exceptions (subclasses of Exception, excluding RuntimeException) must be either caught with try-catch or declared in the method signature with throws — the compiler enforces this. Examples: IOException, SQLException, ParseException. They represent foreseeable, potentially recoverable external failures. Unchecked exceptions (subclasses of RuntimeException or Error) do not require catching or declaration. Examples: NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. They typically represent programming errors that should be fixed, not caught. Modern Java practice: prefer unchecked exceptions in application code — they don't pollute method signatures, and most frameworks (Spring, JPA) convert checked exceptions to unchecked equivalents.

items.q: Q2. Does finally always execute? When does it NOT execute?
items.a: Finally almost always executes — after try (and any matching catch) completes, whether normally, via exception, or via return/break/continue. The three cases where finally does NOT execute: (1) System.exit() is called — it terminates the JVM immediately, bypassing finally. (2) The JVM crashes (OutOfMemoryError at JVM level, kill -9 on the process). (3) A daemon thread is killed when all non-daemon threads finish. In normal application code, finally is guaranteed to run. This is why it's used for resource cleanup and lock release.

items.q: Q3. What is the difference between throw and throws in Java?
items.a: throw is a runtime statement that actually fires an exception: throw new IllegalArgumentException('Invalid input'). It takes a single exception INSTANCE and immediately interrupts execution. throws is a compile-time declaration in a method signature: public void readFile() throws IOException. It takes exception CLASS names (comma-separated) and warns the compiler and callers that these checked exceptions may propagate. One analogy: throws is the warning label on a box ('may contain broken glass'); throw is actually breaking the glass. You use throw to create and fire an exception; you use throws to tell callers they need to handle it.

items.q: Q4. What happens if both try and finally throw exceptions?
items.a: The exception thrown in finally REPLACES the exception thrown in try — the original exception is silently lost. Example: try { throw new IOException('file error'); } finally { throw new RuntimeException('cleanup error'); } — the caller receives only RuntimeException. The IOException is completely invisible. This is why throwing from finally is an anti-pattern — it swallows the original cause. In contrast, try-with-resources handles this correctly: if both the body and close() throw, the body exception is kept as the primary and the close() exception becomes a suppressed exception accessible via e.getSuppressed().

items.q: Q5. What is try-with-resources and what is AutoCloseable?
items.a: Try-with-resources (Java 7+) is a try statement that declares resource objects in its header. Java automatically calls close() on each resource when the block exits — in reverse order of declaration — whether the block exits normally or via exception. Any class implementing java.lang.AutoCloseable (single method: void close() throws Exception) can be used as a resource. Its subinterface java.io.Closeable (close() throws IOException) is used by streams. Java 9+ allows using effectively-final variables declared outside the try: try (existingResource) { }. This eliminates the verbose and error-prone manually-coded finally-based resource cleanup.

items.q: Q6. What is exception chaining and why is it important?
items.a: Exception chaining (wrapping) means catching a lower-level exception and throwing a higher-level exception that carries the original as its cause: throw new ServiceException('Operation failed', originalException). The cause is passed to the exception constructor and accessible via getCause(). Why it's important: (1) Abstraction — service layer doesn't expose SQL or IO implementation details to the web layer. (2) Debugging — the full chain appears in the stack trace: 'Caused by: java.sql.SQLException: ...' makes the root cause visible. (3) Semantic clarity — UserServiceException communicates WHAT failed; the cause shows WHY at the infrastructure level. Without chaining, the original stack trace is lost.

items.q: Q7. Can you catch multiple exception types in one catch block? What is the constraint?
items.a: Yes — Java 7+ introduced multi-catch using the pipe operator: catch (IOException | SQLException e). The constraint: the exception variable 'e' is implicitly final — you cannot reassign it inside the block. Also, the exception types cannot be in a subtype relationship with each other: catch (IOException | FileNotFoundException e) causes a compile error because FileNotFoundException is a subclass of IOException — it would never reach the FileNotFoundException handler independently. Multi-catch generates the same bytecode as separate catch blocks — it's purely a syntax improvement that eliminates copy-paste handling code.

items.q: Q8. How would you design a custom exception hierarchy for an enterprise application?
items.a: Good enterprise exception hierarchy: (1) Base: AppException extends RuntimeException with errorCode field — all application exceptions extend this. (2) Domain layer: InsufficientFundsException, UserNotFoundException, OrderAlreadyProcessedException — extend AppException, carry domain-specific fields. (3) Service layer: PaymentServiceException, InventoryServiceException — translate infrastructure failures. (4) Infrastructure layer: PaymentGatewayException, DatabaseException — wrap third-party/SQL exceptions. (5) API boundary: GlobalExceptionHandler maps domain exceptions to HTTP status codes. Key principles: unchecked at application level (less boilerplate), rich context in exception fields (not just strings), exception code for monitoring/alerting, log ONCE at the boundary.

Output: A followed by B. 'C' never prints. Explanation: 'A' prints normally. The return statement begins to exit the method. Before actually returning, Java executes the finally block — 'B' prints. After finally completes, the original return executes and the method exits. 'C' is unreachable — the compiler may flag it as unreachable code. Key insight: finally executes even when return is encountered inside try. If finally also had a return statement, it would override the try's return — a common exam trap.

items.q: Q10. What is the difference between Error and Exception? Should you ever catch Error?
items.a: Exception represents application-level failures that programs can reasonably handle: file not found, DB connection failed, invalid input. Error represents JVM-level failures that applications generally cannot recover from: OutOfMemoryError (heap exhausted), StackOverflowError (call stack full), VirtualMachineError (JVM internals broken). You should NOT catch Error in application code because: (1) the JVM may be in an inconsistent state — continuing is dangerous. (2) Catching OOM and continuing doesn't free memory — the next allocation fails again. The one legitimate exception: top-level main() or server thread entry points that catch Throwable to log and do a graceful shutdown — but always System.exit() after, never continue. Never catch Error to 'recover' — fix the root cause instead (infinite recursion → fix algorithm, OOM → tune heap).

Three issues: (1) Too broad catch — catching Exception swallows all exceptions including NullPointerException (if input is null), hiding bugs. (2) Returning -1 is ambiguous — is -1 a valid age? Caller cannot distinguish 'parse failed' from 'age is negative'. (3) No logging — failure is completely silent. Fix: public OptionalInt parseAge(String input) { if (input == null || input.isBlank()) return OptionalInt.empty(); try { int age = Integer.parseInt(input.trim()); if (age < 0 || age > 150) return OptionalInt.empty(); return OptionalInt.of(age); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { return OptionalInt.empty(); } }. Better: use specific exception, return Optional/OptionalInt to signal failure explicitly.

The compiler requires this ordering — a more specific subclass catch must appear before its superclass catch. If the order were reversed (IOException first, FileNotFoundException second), the compiler would throw 'exception FileNotFoundException has already been caught' — an unreachable catch block error. Good practice: always order from most specific (deepest subclass) to least specific (shallowest superclass).

The return 20 in finally OVERRIDES the pending return from try. The method returns 20. The original value 10 is discarded. This is why returning from finally is an anti-pattern — it silently discards the try block's return value and masks any exceptions. The compiler does NOT warn about this in most configurations. Always avoid return (and throw) statements in finally blocks.

Double logging anti-pattern. When processOrder() is called from the controller, and the controller also has a global exception handler (like @ControllerAdvice), the same exception stack trace gets logged TWICE: once here and once in the global handler. In a 3-layer app (Controller → Service → Repository), this means 2-3 identical stack traces per failure in your logs — making them unreadable. Fix: either just rethrow without logging (let the boundary handler log once): throw e; OR log and DON'T rethrow (swallow at this layer): log.error(); return; OR wrap in a domain exception (no logging here, boundary handler logs): throw new OrderPersistenceException('Save failed', e). Choose ONE place to log each exception.

sections.title: Conclusion — Exception Handling: The Difference Between Brittle and Robust Code

blocks.text: Exception handling is where the quality gap between junior and senior Java developers is most visible. Junior code swallows exceptions, returns null from catch blocks, catches Exception broadly, and logs-then-rethrows at every layer. Senior code uses specific exceptions, carries domain context in custom exception fields, chains causes for full stack visibility, logs exactly once at the boundary, and uses try-with-resources for all resource management.

The most important insight about exception handling is that it is ultimately about communication — between the code that detects a problem and the code (or human) that needs to respond. A catch(Exception e){} block says 'something went wrong but I'm hiding it from everyone.' A PaymentGatewayException with isRetryable(), getGatewayErrorCode(), and a chained cause says exactly what failed, why, and what to do about it.

items.q: What is exception handling in Java?
items.a: Exception handling in Java is the structured mechanism for detecting, responding to, and recovering from runtime errors without crashing the program. Java uses five keywords: try (marks risky code), catch (handles specific exception types), finally (always-runs cleanup), throw (manually fires an exception), throws (declares propagated checked exceptions). The model separates error-handling code from business logic, making programs more readable, maintainable, and resilient.

items.q: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions in Java?
items.a: Checked exceptions (subclasses of Exception, not RuntimeException) must be caught or declared with throws — the compiler enforces this. Examples: IOException, SQLException. They represent foreseeable external failures callers should handle. Unchecked exceptions (subclasses of RuntimeException or Error) require no declaration or catching. Examples: NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException. They typically represent programming errors to be fixed. Modern practice: use unchecked exceptions in application code to keep method signatures clean.

items.q: What is the difference between throw and throws in Java?
items.a: throw is a runtime statement that actually fires an exception: throw new IOException('File missing'). It takes a single exception instance and immediately interrupts execution. throws is a compile-time method signature declaration: public void readFile() throws IOException. It lists exception class names and informs the compiler and callers that these checked exceptions may propagate. throw executes something; throws declares something.

items.q: What is try-with-resources in Java?
items.a: Try-with-resources (Java 7+) automatically closes resources declared in the try header when the block exits — whether normally or via exception. Resources must implement AutoCloseable. Multiple resources are closed in reverse order of declaration. This eliminates verbose finally-based cleanup code. If both the body and close() throw, the close() exception is suppressed (attached to primary, accessible via getSuppressed()) — unlike plain finally where the original exception is silently lost.

items.q: Does finally always execute in Java?
items.a: Almost always. Finally executes after try and any matching catch complete — whether the block exits normally, via exception, or via return/break/continue. Three exceptions: System.exit() terminates the JVM immediately (finally skipped); JVM crash (OutOfMemoryError at JVM level); daemon thread killed when all non-daemon threads finish. In normal application code, finally is guaranteed to run — which is why it's used for lock release, connection cleanup, and other guaranteed-cleanup operations.
